content: The area of community detection encompasses a variety of graph partitioning approaches which aim to find `good' partitions into subgraphs (or communities) according to different cost functions, without imposing the number of communities a priori BIBREF31 . The notion of community thus depends on the choice of cost function. Commonly, communities are taken to be subgraphs whose nodes are connected strongly within the community with relatively weak inter-community edges. Such structural notion is related to balanced cuts. Other cost functions are posed in terms of transitions inside and outside of the communities, usually as one-step processes BIBREF4 . When transition paths of random walks of all lengths are considered, the concept of community becomes intrinsically multi-scale, i.e., different partitions can be found to be relevant at different time scales leading to a multi-level description dictated by the transition dynamics BIBREF9 , BIBREF32 , BIBREF10 . This leads to the framework of Markov Stability, a dynamics-based, multi-scale community detection methodology, which can be shown to recover seamlessly several well-known heuristics as particular cases BIBREF9 , BIBREF11 , BIBREF12 .
